What should the project team do?

options.text: Use a variety of user stories to ensure the project meets the most relevant customer expectations, even amid market volatility.
Schedule adequate buffers and reserves in the project management plan to ensure the project team has time to react to any unforeseen hurdles.
Implement iterative feedback mechanisms to allow readjustments to real-time external inputs and ensure delivered value remains high.
Organize a contingency reserve to cover the costs and time required to respond to any major environmental changes.

questions.solutionLine: C. Implement iterative feedback mechanisms to allow readjustments to real-time external inputs and ensure delivered value remains high.
questions.explanation:
In industries characterized by high dynamism, such as financial technology, projects must be managed flexibly to adjust to rapidly evolving external factors. Incorporating iterative feedback mechanisms allows scope adjustments to real-time external inputs and enables the project team to continuously refine and realign the project’s objectives to maintain relevance and ensure the delivered value remains high.

The other options do not guarantee flexibility or ensure the project team can adapt quickly to changing market conditions.

Although it can be useful to have a variety of user stories in the backlog to work with, no project team can predict every technological advance or market fluctuation that occurs throughout the course of the project. Without an iterative approach in place to react to such hurdles, having a large variety of inputs will not be beneficial to adapting to changing market conditions.

Scheduling buffers and reserves into the project management plan can give the project team more space in which to react to real-time external inputs, but this does not guarantee flexibility on its own. If the project team does not use that time to iterate and adapt the project scope, it is likely that the project’s delivery schedule will still be negatively impacted.

Organizing a contingency reserve in the project budget will be useful only if the project team has correctly assessed the risks and challenges that may arise and has an effective plan in place to react to them accordingly. Unexpected developments are not typically covered in the contingency reserve, and without iterative feedback mechanisms, there is no guarantee that the project team can react quickly and efficiently to the new inputs.

questions.stem:
The project manager is responsible for a major project that involves working with many vendors. A key project concern is ensuring the quality and timely delivery of products and services procured from vendors.

What should the project manager do to ensure the delivery stays on schedule?

options.text: Raise an item in the risk register to capture potential impacts related to delays in the procurement of products and services, mitigating the risk of suboptimal quality.
Conduct regular procurement performance reviews with all vendors to ensure that products and services are delivered on time and in accordance with the contract.
Delegate the management of the procurement process and vendor management to the procurement department because they have the tools to deal with a large number of vendors.
Review the vendor management plan with all selected vendors before the contract period begins to ensure compliance and confirm that they agree with the plan.

questions.solutionLine: B. Conduct regular procurement performance reviews with all vendors to ensure that products and services are delivered on time and in accordance with the contract.
questions.explanation:
By conducting procurement performance reviews on a regular basis, the project manager can proactively identify and address any potential issues with vendor performance. This will help ensure that the project meets its procurement objectives and that the products are delivered on time and meet the quality requirements.

The other options are incorrect.

Updating the risk register is important in general, but it does not directly respond to the quality and delivery time issue.

Delegating the work to procurement will ensure that vendors abide by the contract terms, but this is not enough to guarantee that the products meet the quality requirements and are delivered on time.

Reviewing the vendor management plan will not be enough to identify and address any potential problems as the work progresses. It is essential to ensure alignment with vendors, but this should be part of a comprehensive process for monitoring their performance.

questions.stem:
A project is in its second month of execution and follows a hybrid delivery model. A key team member responsible for integrating two critical system components was unexpectedly reassigned by their functional manager. A replacement was assigned immediately, but the new team member lacks domain expertise and onboarding will take time. A key stakeholder, who is also the product sponsor, expresses concern about timeline slippage and questions the team’s ability to deliver the next milestone.

What should the project manager do to maintain delivery momentum and address the stakeholder’s concern?

options.text: Request the functional manager to reassign the former team member for critical integration tasks.
Update the risk register and discuss the impact with the sponsor at the next scheduled checkpoint.
Review the milestone plan, adjust assignments based on capacity, and align on mitigation actions.
Escalate the concern to the PMO and seek additional resources for this project phase.

questions.solutionLine: C. Review the milestone plan, adjust assignments based on capacity, and align on mitigation actions.
questions.explanation:
Reviewing the milestone plan, realigning assignments based on actual team capacity, and agreeing with the team on mitigation actions shows proactive, adaptive planning. This approach helps sustain delivery momentum while directly addressing stakeholder concerns in a transparent and collaborative way.

The other options are incorrect.

Reassigning the former team member may not be feasible and bypasses the functional manager's authority. It also does not build long-term resilience in the team.

While updating the risk register is necessary, waiting for the next scheduled checkpoint delays action. It does not immediately address the delivery risk or stakeholder concern.

Escalating to the PMO and seeking more resources may be premature. It suggests the team cannot handle the challenge without first attempting internal adjustments and mitigation.

questions.stem:
During project execution, the project manager is considering how to identify the expectations of the project’s internal and external customers. What the stakeholders value and how they define success is important for the success of the project. The project manager needs to achieve a full understanding that can reliably guide the project.

What should the project manager do?

options.text: Analyze the stakeholders’ information, weighing their expectations against their involvement, influence, and potential impact.
Survey the stakeholders, asking them to list their interests and concerns for the project, and document the responses for reference.
Invite all stakeholders to a kickoff meeting, offering everyone an equal opportunity to discuss their expectations with the team.
Prioritize the expectations of external customers over internal stakeholders to ensure the most effective use of financial resources.

questions.solutionLine: A. Analyze the stakeholders’ information, weighing their expectations against their involvement, influence, and potential impact.
questions.explanation:
The project manager and team should engage with stakeholders in multiple ways to discover and document their expectations. The next step, however, should be to analyze the collected information, considering the relative importance, power, and influence of each stakeholder. That analysis is the key to clarifying the project’s priorities.

The other options are incorrect.

A survey could be a useful tool for gathering information. However, a survey alone would not provide enough information to produce a truly helpful reference.

A meeting would be a good opportunity for the stakeholders to discuss their expectations, and especially to engage with each other about differences in their expectations. However, further analysis would be needed to turn the input into meaningful guidance for the project.

Finding a way to prioritize potentially competing expectations is a critical task for the project manager. However, prioritizing financial clout alone might be inadequate and misleading about the right direction for the project. The manager should consider all factors in weighing the stakeholders’ expectations.

questions.stem:
A product manufacturer is developing a new product. The project sponsor proposes reducing the number of inspection steps due to budget pressure. The quality assurance manager warns that this could potentially increase the risk of defects. The client reaffirms that quality must be preserved. The finance controller emphasizes that savings are necessary for the project's financial viability.

What should the project manager do?

options.text: Limit inspection steps to save money, with the understanding that defects will likely increase later.
Defer inspections until later phases, balancing short-term savings against higher defect risks.
Streamline inspection steps by identifying and eliminating redundancy rather than reducing them.
Retain full inspections to preserve quality, explaining the trade-offs clearly to the stakeholders.

questions.solutionLine: D. Retain full inspections to preserve quality, explaining the trade-offs clearly to the stakeholders.
questions.explanation:
The project manager should protect quality despite cost pressure. By retaining full inspections and clearly communicating the associated trade-offs, stakeholders understand the impact on schedule, cost, or resources while maintaining confidence in the project’s quality outcomes.

The other options are incorrect.

Limiting inspections to save money is not responsible and undermines quality and compliance.

Deferring inspections is not proactive, increases risks, and exposes the project to hidden or compounding defects.

Redundant processes, such as overlapping tests or multiple QA teams reviewing the same output, can help catch errors or defects that might have been missed by a single method or individual.

questions.stem:
A project team adopted agile practices to meet the business need to develop an application. One of the senior team members inconsistently attends the team meetings, including the daily standup meetings. This senior team member then requests other team members to provide status updates on his/her behalf during the stand up meetings.

What should the project manager do to handle this situation?

options.text: Request the removal of the senior team member due to the participation issues.
Remind the senior team member to adhere to the team's working agreement.
Escalate the senior team member's participation to upper management.
Request the other team members to cover the tasks assigned to the senior team member.

questions.solutionLine: B. Remind the senior team member to adhere to the team's working agreement.
questions.explanation:
The project manager should remind the senior team member of the team's working agreement and ensure they stick to it.

All other options are incorrect.

Having other team members cover is also not sustainable and affects team dynamics.

The project manager should first try to resolve this situation with the senior team member.

Removal requests are a form of escalation and is done only if the Project Manager is unable to resolve the current issue.

questions.stem:
A project team is drafting the first version of their budget. The team members understand the need for adding a contingency reserve to cover budget overruns. However, the project manager wants to avoid using contingency funds.

What should the project manager do?

options.text: Set up the contingency reserve outside the initial project budget and manage the reserve separately.
Manage the contingency reserve implicitly by making it part of the budget's cost basis.
Reduce the contingency reserve amount as the project progresses and more information becomes available.
Work to proactively anticipate threats that might damage the budget and affect the contingency reserve.

questions.solutionLine: D. Work to proactively anticipate threats that might damage the budget and affect the contingency reserve.
questions.explanation:
Taking a proactive stance toward anticipating and preventing threats to the budget can help the project team avoid having to use the contingency funds. Although it is impossible to control every unknown factor, this approach has the best chance of keeping the contingency reserve intact.

The other options are incorrect.

Separating the contingency reserve from the initial project budget might be a useful way to manage it in some cases. However, the separation would not establish safeguards to prevent the need for using it.

Including the contingency reserve as part of the budget’s cost basis is a common approach, but this way of managing the reserve does not affect whether the funds will ever be needed.

Reducing the contingency reserve as more project stages are completed would gradually free up funds, but it would not prevent unexpected problems.

questions.stem:
A project manager is assigned to a project in a country where the company has no prior business experience. At the beginning of the project, the project manager realizes that there may be local regulatory requirements that the project team has no experience with.

What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Assign sufficient budget in case such requirements must be met.
Consult with a subject matter expert (SME) on how to avoid such requirements.
Engage a subject matter expert (SME) to check if the requirements are relevant.
Escalate concerns about the requirements to the project sponsor.

questions.solutionLine: C. Engage a subject matter expert (SME) to check if the requirements are relevant.
questions.explanation:
When encountering unfamiliar regulatory requirements in a new country, consulting a subject matter expert to evaluate their relevance helps avoid unnecessary costs and compliance efforts, while ensuring that actual requirements are properly met. This approach provides accurate information before making strategic decisions.

The other options are incorrect.

Assigning a budget allocates resources without understanding the requirements, their impact, or whether they are relevant to the project.

Focusing on avoiding requirements rather than understanding compliance obligations and their relevance is irresponsible.

Escalating concerns to the project sponsor at this stage is not effective and may not be necessary. The project manager should consider escalation after assessing the situation and obtaining an expert evaluation to support informed decisions.

questions.stem:
At the midway point in a project's execution, the finance director announces a 15% budget cut across all aspects of the project. The project sponsor pressures the project manager to protect high-visibility deliverables, although the technical lead warns that quality could be compromised as a result of the cuts. The finance team insists adjustments must be formally assessed before work continues.

What should the project manager do?

options.text: Reduce the scope to meet the new budget without documenting the change.
Shift financial responsibility to the operations department to maintain the current scope.
Ask the sponsor to decide which deliverables can be removed without affecting the project.
Adjust the project baseline with stakeholder alignment and governance approval.

questions.solutionLine: D. Adjust the project baseline with stakeholder alignment and governance approval.
questions.explanation:
The project manager should execute structured re-baselining with governance. Aligning with stakeholders and obtaining governance approval maintains transparency, accountability, and project control while keeping objectives realistic and achievable.

The other options are incorrect.

Adjusting the scope should be reviewed and justified through a collaborative, well-documented process. Otherwise, it would create misalignment and scope creep.

Informal cost shifting undermines transparency.

The project sponsor cannot make the decision alone, so the project manager must facilitate the analysis.

questions.stem:
After acquiring a competitor, a large conglomerate is enforcing enterprise project management standards across all corporate initiatives. A project team has been assigned to rebrand the acquired company’s product line, but several stakeholders disagree about the rebranding direction. Their conflict is creating tension within the integration effort. The project sponsor is concerned that stakeholder resistance could undermine the successful cultural and operational alignment of the new organization.

What should the project manager do?

options.text: Develop a stakeholder engagement strategy that ensures alignment with the acquiring company’s culture and integration objectives.
Continue executing according to the enterprise project management standards to maintain adherence to schedule and delivery commitments.
Schedule a facilitated session with stakeholders to clarify the sources of disagreement and evaluate the impact on project execution.
Meet with the sponsor to better understand the organizational integration concerns and request direction on handling stakeholder resistance.

questions.solutionLine: A. Develop a stakeholder engagement strategy that ensures alignment with the acquiring company’s culture and integration objectives.
questions.explanation:
Executing a stakeholder engagement plan provides a proactive, structured approach to aligning resistant stakeholders with the acquiring company’s culture and integration goals.

The other options are incorrect.

Continuing execution according to standards emphasizes compliance with new standards and delivery discipline but ignores stakeholder resistance, which is a major risk to integration success.

Facilitating a stakeholder session is helpful as a tactic, but the project manager should prioritize a formal engagement strategy over an ad hoc meeting.

Meeting the sponsor is an overreliance on the sponsor instead of the project manager actively managing stakeholder engagement.

questions.stem:
A software development company is developing a new revision for an existing product. During system integration, two functional managers dispute ownership of a major interface. The requirements document is vague, and the work breakdown structure (WBS) lists the component under multiple packages. The client complains about the delays and alleges poor accountability. The sponsor pressures the project manager to assign ownership to one of the functional managers, warning that the dispute could lead to audit issues.

What should the project manager do?

options.text: Clarify ownership by updating the WBS dictionary and realigning responsibilities with stakeholder agreement.
Assign ownership to the team’s functional manager with a stronger technical capacity to restore progress quickly.
Revise the requirements document and the WBS to clarify management roles and add a definition of ownership.
Divide ownership responsibilities among the project team to reduce audit issues and increase accountability.

questions.solutionLine: A. Clarify ownership by updating the WBS dictionary and realigning responsibilities with stakeholder agreement.
questions.explanation:
The project manager needs to resolve ambiguities quickly using scope tools (e.g., the WBS dictionary). The WBS dictionary provides detailed documentation for each work package, including who is responsible for its completion. Functional managers, team members, and stakeholders can refer to the dictionary to understand their specific roles and responsibilities, reducing confusion and overlap.

The other options are incorrect.

Quick assignment ignores structural ambiguity.

Assignments should be based on project needs rather than subjective preferences or external pressures.

Revising the documents for clarity bypasses the project manager’s accountability.

Dividing ownership risks duplication, rework, and defects. Accountability becomes diluted when multiple people share ownership, as it may be unclear who is responsible for ensuring quality standards are met.

questions.stem:
A hybrid project involving many stakeholders is underway. As requested by the project management office (PMO), the project status reports, as well as other project documents, are being stored in a central repository. When reviewing the documents stored in the repository, the project manager discovered that documents were either not updated or were missing.

What should the project manager do?

options.text: Discuss the situation with the project sponsor to reduce the level of documentation.
Work with the team leaders to update the required project reports.
Stop all project activities until the project documents are updated and uploaded
Schedule a knowledge transfer session at the final stage of the project.

questions.solutionLine: B. Work with the team leaders to update the required project reports.
questions.explanation:
The first step to address missing or poor documentation would be to correct the deficiency. Then the project manager should work with the team to ensure that documentation procedures are followed and required project reports are updated.

The other options are incorrect.

Discussing the problem with the sponsor is incorrect, as it falls within the project manager's authority to remedy.

The project manager does not need to stop all other project activities to address this issue.

Project documentation should be updated, and knowledge should be transferred throughout the project, not just at the final stage of the project.

questions.stem:
During a quality audit of a complex infrastructure project, the auditor identifies that risk review meetings lack proper attendance documentation, making it impossible to verify stakeholder engagement in critical risk decisions. The project team has developed and implemented corrective actions for the attendance documentation process, but stakeholder attendance remains inconsistent.

What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Provide legal documentation requiring stakeholder participation in risk decision-making processes.
Coach stakeholders on the importance of accountability and traceability for effective risk management.
Implement detailed measurement protocols to assess the effectiveness of stakeholder engagement.
Support the auditor by requesting their recommendation and escalating the issue to the project sponsor.

questions.solutionLine: B. Coach stakeholders on the importance of accountability and traceability for effective risk management.
questions.explanation:
Coaching stakeholders will help address the engagement issue directly, build awareness, and strengthen participation. This will help ensure that stakeholders are adequately engaged in risk management processes, accountability is clear, and similar issues are avoided in the future.

The other options are incorrect.

Focusing on legal documentation at this stage may be excessive and emphasizes strict legal actions rather than solving the problem in a positive way by educating and coaching stakeholders. The stakeholders might not understand the significance of attending risk review meetings, so the project manager should clarify it for them.

Implementing detailed measurement protocols emphasizes process metrics rather than the fundamental need for accountability, traceability, and stakeholder education. This may also lead to unnecessary and time-consuming documentation policies.

Requesting the auditor’s recommendation is unnecessary for addressing stakeholder engagement. Escalation is only needed if the project manager can't reach a resolution. The project manager should first try to address stakeholder behavior through engagement and coaching.

questions.stem:
A project manager has received quotes from two vendors for the same parts. Vendor A has informed the project manager that they fulfilled a similar order two months ago at a price that was 2% under the original planned cost. Vendor B has a history of on-time delivery but has announced a price increase.

How should the project manager evaluate this situation?

options.text: Review the agreements and procurement documentation for Vendor B to force them to keep the original pricing.
Evaluate previous contract clauses from Vendor B and decrease orders, prioritizing orders from Vendor A whenever possible.
Use the metrics from Vendor A to request better pricing from Vendor B, keeping both providers as a risk mitigation strategy.
Review the work performance information of both vendors against their contracts to find the preferred supplier.

questions.solutionLine: D. Review the work performance information of both vendors against their contracts to find the preferred supplier.
questions.explanation:
To make an informed supplier decision, the project manager should review the work performance information of both vendors against their contracts first. This allows a data-driven assessment of quality, delivery, cost, and compliance. Choosing a vendor based solely on price ignores critical performance factors.

The other options are incorrect.

It is unrealistic to force Vendor B to keep the original pricing if pricing terms allow adjustments.

Reducing the orders from Vendor B may breach contract terms and harm vendor relations.

Requesting better pricing from Vendor B assumes comparability and may strain negotiations without guaranteed results.

questions.stem:
The agile team is midway through the current sprint. One team member is working on a user story required to deliver a critical functionality for the sprint goal. During daily coordination meetings, the team member has given vague updates, such as "still progressing," for several days in a row. No visible progress has been made, and the functionality is now at risk. Other team members are unaware of the exact blockers, and the product owner is becoming concerned about the sprint outcome.

What should the project manager do to address this situation and protect sprint goals?

options.text: Ask the team to collectively support the developer in completing the story before the sprint ends.
Meet one-on-one with the team member to understand the issue and agree on a course of action.
Escalate the issue to the product owner and propose replacing the user story with a simpler one.
Immediately reassign the story to another team member to avoid missing the sprint commitment.

questions.solutionLine: B. Meet one-on-one with the team member to understand the issue and agree on a course of action.
questions.explanation:
In agile, the project manager (or scrum master) should address potential blockers early. A private, supportive conversation can help uncover the real issue and co-create a solution, maintaining trust and team cohesion.

The other options are incorrect.

Team collaboration is important, but without first understanding the blocker, blindly assigning support may not resolve the root cause.

By escalating issues to the product owner and swapping out the story without first investigating the root cause, the project manager bypasses their servant leadership responsibilities and risks affecting the project's scope expectations.

Reassigning the work immediately might demotivate the team member and damage psychological safety. This should be a last resort after attempting to understand the situation.

questions.stem:
Shortly after a sprint kickoff, the project manager receives an email from a key stakeholder who raises a serious concern and insists on modifying one deliverable that is already in progress.

What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Address the request during the daily scrum and request suggestions from the team about the change.
Immediately modify the backlog and instruct the team to start working on the requested deliverable.
Schedule a meeting with the stakeholder and product owner to discuss and evaluate the request.
Cancel the current sprint, hold a retrospective, and invite the stakeholder to discuss the change.

questions.solutionLine: C. Schedule a meeting with the stakeholder and product owner to discuss and evaluate the request.
questions.explanation:
A meeting with the stakeholder and product owner encourages open discussion to clearly understand feasibility, impact, prioritization, and alignment before making changes, reducing disruptions and promoting collaboration.

The other options are incorrect.

Addressing the request at the daily scrum and asking the team is premature and inappropriate, as the daily scrum is intended for internal team coordination, not for resolving stakeholder issues or prioritization.

Immediately modifying the backlog and instructing the team bypasses proper agile governance, risks uncontrolled scope changes, and disruption of sprint commitments.

Canceling the current sprint is an extreme and rarely justified step for a single concern early in the sprint. Sprint cancellation should be reserved for severe, project-wide issues.

questions.stem:
A consumer electronics company is executing a project to produce a new line of smart home sensors. During quality reviews, the quality assurance department reports that additional testing and environmentally friendly packaging will increase upfront costs but reduce warranty claims and environmental impact. The operations manager argues against adding these steps in order to stay on budget. With the product launch approaching, the project manager is under pressure to resolve the issue quickly.

What should the project manager do?

options.text: Facilitate a resolution workshop between quality assurance and operations departments to reach consensus on the chosen path forward.
Evaluate the cost of quality and sustainability tradeoffs and request a corresponding change to the quality management plan if warranted.
Prioritize the long-term benefits recommended by the quality assurance manager and evaluate changes to the project management plan.
Add both the quality assurance and the operations recommendations to the project management plan to meet the launch deadline efficiently.

questions.solutionLine: B. Evaluate cost of quality and sustainability tradeoffs and request a corresponding change to the quality management plan if warranted.
questions.explanation:
The project manager should first analyze the cost of quality and sustainability tradeoffs, and then, if justified, request a change to the quality management plan through integrated change control. This option reflects both the principle of evaluation and the governance requirement for plan updates.

The other options are incorrect.

Although facilitation and conflict resolution are valid tools, the project manager’s responsibility here is not to mediate until consensus is reached but to evaluate tradeoffs and apply integrated change control. This option distracts by sounding collaborative, but it fails to address governance.

Prioritizing the quality assurance manager’s recommendation and evaluating the project management plan changes favors this view. It skips a balanced evaluation and does not explicitly follow change control to update the plan.

Adding both recommendations to the project management plan to address urgency looks efficient under urgency, but omits the necessary evaluation and does not explicitly follow change control to update the plan.

questions.stem:
A project manager decided to award additional work to the current contractor to reduce procurement time during a bidding process. The other bidders complained that the process lacked transparency and fairness.

What should the project manager have done to prevent this?

options.text: Invited all potential bidders to a pre-bid meeting to clarify requirements and evaluation criteria.
Awarded the contract to the incumbent contractor after informal talks to speed up the process.
Followed the company’s formal bidding and procurement process procedures strictly.
Provided detailed feedback to all unsuccessful bidders after the contract was awarded.

questions.solutionLine: C. Followed the company’s formal bidding and procurement process procedures strictly.
questions.explanation:
Following established bidding and procurement procedures ensures that the process is conducted fairly, transparently, and consistently. It guarantees that all potential bidders have an equal opportunity to compete and that contract awards are based on objective, and pre-defined criteria. Adherence to these procedures aligns with standard practices for procurement management, promoting fairness, stakeholder trust, and legal compliance.

The other options are incorrect.

Inviting all potential bidders to a pre-bid meeting helps clarify requirements but does not replace the need to follow formal bidding procedures for fairness and transparency.

Awarding the contract after informal talks bypasses formal processes and may raise concerns of favoritism and unfair advantage.

Providing feedback after contract award is good practice for transparency, but it does not prevent unfairness or complaints during the actual bidding and awarding process.

questions.stem:
A project’s financial plan is being developed. The financial planner has requested relevant documentation to help align specific deliverables and work packages with estimated costs.

What information should the project manager provide?

options.text: The work breakdown structure (WBS).
The resource breakdown structure (RBS).
The organizational breakdown structure (OBS).
The value breakdown structure (VBS).

questions.solutionLine: A. The work breakdown structure (WBS).
questions.explanation:
The WBS serves as the foundation for budgeting by aligning specific deliverables and work packages with their estimated costs. Breaking the project into smaller, manageable units helps project managers and financial planners allocate funds precisely to components, track expenses effectively, and identify cost drivers. It also helps when integrating scope, schedule, and cost baselines to ensure clear alignment across all project management components.

The other options are incorrect.

While additional documents and information might be helpful, they would not directly meet the need on their own.

The RBS is a hierarchical representation of resources by category and type. The RBS is used in conjunction with the WBS to plan, monitor, and control the work.

The OBS is a hierarchical representation of the project organization that illustrates the relationships between project activities and the organizational units that will perform them.

The VBS focuses on breaking down a project's value rather than just its work or deliverables. It decomposes stakeholders’ value expectations into value items to ensure that all project activities are directly aligned with delivering stakeholder-defined value.

questions.stem:
An adaptative project team is globally distributed and the team members speak different primary languages. Daily meetings are conducted virtually in a common language. The project manager is made aware that there are some communication issues. Differences in pronunciation, accent, and vocabulary make it extremely difficult for some members to understand each other.

What should the project manager do to improve the daily meeting and avoid misunderstanding?

options.text: Use the call to verbally summarize the work status as reported by the team members.
Use an electronic task board to give a visual representation of work status and progress.
Ask for a change in the project's budget to provide access to a translation service.
Ask all team members to report on work completed, upcoming work, and blockers.

questions.solutionLine: B. Use an electronic task board to give a visual representation of work status and progress.
questions.explanation:
Visual tools like task boards serve as information radiators, helping teams overcome language barriers by providing clear, accessible, translatable updates that don’t rely on verbal precision. This aligns with agile values of collaboration, visibility, and continuous improvement.

All other options are incorrect.

Using the call to summarize the work status increases reliance on verbal communication, which is already problematic due to accents and vocabulary differences.

Adding translation services suggests a costly and complex solution that contradicts agile’s preference for lightweight, low-cost tools.

Asking team members to report is not addressing the root issue - it does not tailor the method to resolve communication gaps caused by linguistic challenges.
